title: Bathing with Nature – A Forest Walk Experience
summary: A half-day forest bathing walk at Bukit Timah Nature Reserve where youths put their phones away and embrace nature through a nature walk, sensory booklet tasks, team station games and outdoor tea appreciation. Participants get attuned to their senses and surroundings, learn to regulate emotions and embrace the discomfort of being out in nature, and experience new sights, sounds and smells in a world not normally viewed.

youthNeed:
Today’s youths are growing up in a world increasingly sealed away from the outdoors. Researchers have observed a quiet crisis: the more time young people spend indoors, the more their emotional, mental, and physical health suffers. Lowered immunity, rising rates of depression, and heightened irritability have all been linked to nature deficiency. Perhaps most concerning, a lack of outdoor exposure lowers their tolerance to stress—meaning that when challenges arise, their internal reserves are already depleted.

At the same time, stress levels among youths are at an all-time high. Record numbers report anxiety, depression, and a sense of being overwhelmed. Yet society offers few healthy outlets. Peer pressure, personal image concerns, and the constant performance of online life leave them with nowhere safe to simply be. They long to express themselves and unburden their struggles, but the avenues for doing so are shrinking.

How It Responds to Youths’ Primary Challenges

Emotional and Mental Overload
Bathing with Nature provides an outlet that asks nothing in return. Unlike social media, which demands performance, or academics, which demand results, the forest demands only presence. This lowers anxiety by replacing constant stimulation with gentle awareness. Youths learn, without being taught, that they can feel difficult emotions without judgment—and that those feelings often soften when held in a calm, natural space.

Low Stress Tolerance
Repeated exposure to nature has been shown to build resilience. As youths walk the same trail over multiple sessions, they encounter small stressors (uneven ground, changing weather, momentary discomfort) in a low-stakes environment. Over time, their nervous systems learn to recover more quickly—a skill that transfers directly to school, home, and social life.

Lack of Safe, Secure Outlets for Expression
In the forest, there is no peer hierarchy. No one is watching to see if they “look cool.” The trees do not judge. This safety allows youths to speak, cry, laugh, or remain silent without fear. Facilitators are trained to hold space without forcing conversation. For many, this becomes the first place where they can exhale fully—venting struggles they cannot name elsewhere.

Disconnection from Self and the Present
Constant digital connection has fragmented attention. Bathing with Nature rebuilds the capacity for focus by removing distractions. When a teenager notices the pattern of lichen on a rock or the sound of a stream, they are practicing active, present-moment awareness—a direct antidote to the scattered, overstimulated mind.
whyItMatters:
Youths today are not broken—they are starved of the environments that humans evolved to thrive in. Bathing with Nature does not claim to solve every problem, but it offers something increasingly rare: a low-cost, high-impact intervention that addresses multiple challenges at once. It lowers cortisol, builds stress tolerance, provides emotional safety, and restores attention—all without medication, diagnosis, or digital interface.

In a world that constantly asks young people to do more, this activity invites them to be still. And in that stillness, surrounded by green and growing things, they often find exactly what they have been searching for: themselves.
competencyHow:
The primary focus of the activity is exposure to outdoors for emotional regulation, learning to attune to senses and to embrace the uncomfortability of being out in nature.

Participants will be encouraged to switch off from their outside world, keeping phones and living in the moment. They will go through a series of activities including, a nature walk, outdoor tea appreciation and sensory mapping. Through the use of nature as the medium, they will get attuned to their senses, finding out things about themselves and allowing themselves to explore and interact with the nature around them freely. As they do this, they become more aware of their surroundings, and themselves as well.

mainActivities:
Nature walk/forest bathing experience
Participants to meet at Bukit Timah Nature Reserve main entrance.
Participants will be first encouraged to store their phones away, either keeping it in their bags, or in a keep safe bag for the rest of the activity.
Participants will then be introduced to their Forest Buddy Pack, a mindfulness nature kit consisting of a booklet, stickers, markers and a small pack of tea leaves.
After explaining the booklet and its purpose, Facilitators will commence the walk, which is a series of checkpoints with tasks for participants to do. A total of 4 stations will be marked out, each with its own mini activity.
Whilst on the road, participants will also be tasked to complete the booklet.
Completion will award participant with a reward (notebook)

The book will consist of 5 different activities

Take a photo of 5 different animals/insects

Station Games
For the youth outing, the specific details are as followed:

Activity 1: Photo Challenge
Objective: Teams are tasked with replicating a series of provided group pose photographs with accuracy and creativity.
Mechanics:
A set of pose reference images will be distributed to each team.
Teams must recreate as many poses as possible within a designated time frame.
Points are awarded based on the number of poses successfully completed, as well as the precision and originality of each recreation.
Materials Required: Camera or smartphone, pose reference sheets.
Key Skills Emphasized: Communication, coordination, and attention to detail.

Activity 2: Tarp Flip
Objective: Teams must fold a tarp into the smallest possible area while all members remain standing on it throughout the process.
Mechanics:
Participants begin standing on a fully unfolded tarp.
Without stepping off the tarp at any point, the team must collaboratively fold it into progressively smaller squares.
The activity concludes when the team successfully achieves the smallest fold possible, or when time expires.
Materials Required: One large tarp per team.
Key Skills Emphasized: Problem-solving, balance, spatial awareness, and teamwork.

Activity 3: Lava Crossing
Objective: Teams must navigate an obstacle course from a designated start point to an end point without any participant touching the ground (the "lava").
Mechanics:
Teams are provided with a set of materials (e.g., planks, ropes, or foam tiles) to create pathways across the course.
Participants must strategize and work together to move themselves and their materials forward while avoiding ground contact.
If any participant touches the ground, the team incurs a penalty or must restart from a checkpoint.
Materials Required: Obstacle course layout, provided crossing materials.
Key Skills Emphasized: Strategic planning, resource management, trust, and physical coordination.

Activity 4: Bull Ring
Objective: Teams must transport balls of varying sizes across a fixed distance using only a system of strings held by participants.
Mechanics:
Each participant is given a string attached to a central ring or platform.
By collectively manipulating their strings, the team must lift, balance, and move the balls from a starting point to a designated target area.
The activity is complete when all balls have been successfully transported without dropping any.
Materials Required: Strings, central ring/platform, assorted balls of different sizes and weights.
Key Skills Emphasized: Precision, synchronization, patience, and collective focus.

Activity 5: Helium Straw
Objective: As a team, participants must lower a lightweight straw to the ground while ensuring all members maintain continuous contact with it using only their index fingers.
Mechanics:
The straw is initially placed at chest height, with each participant extending one index finger to support it from underneath.
The team must work together to slowly and evenly lower the straw to the ground.
If any participant loses contact with the straw at any point, the team must restart from the initial height.
Materials Required: One lightweight drinking straw per team.
Key Skills Emphasized: Patience, non-verbal communication, steady coordination, and mutual trust.

For main activities during the programme, we will be using 3 out of the 5 activities depending on the group size and weather on the day itself.

iceSteps:
Sit everyone in a circle
Choose one person to be “it” in the center of the circle. The person in the center of the circle gets the rolled up newspaper. Their objective is for the person in the middle to hit the person in the surrounding circle whose name has been called, before that person can call another name. (All hits must be on the legs only!)
There are three rules regarding the names:
You cannot call the same person who called you
You cannot call the name of the person in the center of the circle, and
the name of the person you call must be present in the circle.
Begin with introductions: Each person in the circle gives their name and possibly one interesting fact about themselves. You can give them a question to answer like “What is your favorite ice-cream?” or questions related to a lesson you plan to do.
After everyone has introduced themselves, explain the rules.
Then call out the name of a person… i.e. “Ken”. Ken must call the name of another person in the circle BEFORE the person in the middle “Whacks” him with the newspaper.
If the person called another name, that person must then call a name, continuing until someone gets “whacked” before they call a name or until someone breaks one of the rules or makes a mistake.
When someone is “whacked” or breaks a rule / makes a mistake they must move to the center of the circle.
The person who just came out of the circle begins the next round by calling a name.
We usually play it so that if you end up in the center of the circle three times, you must perform some kind of “forfeit” such as sing a song, do a dance, tell a joke, etc.

Real or Not
Participants log on to Kahoot and enter the game pin as shown on the screen
Answer questions as a team and achieve the highest cumulative score to get a prize

The "Real or Not" game format on Kahoot is highly suitable for teenagers (ages 13–19) because it leverages their digital literacy, sparks healthy competition, and addresses their need for social validation without causing anxiety.

sessions.title: Session 1 - Basics of AI App Development
sessions.activities:
1. What even is an app? (20 min) - Demystify how AI turns a sentence into working software, with one live "prompt-to-app" demo to hook the room.
2. Idea sprint (25 min) - Each participant picks a real problem in their life and shapes it into a one-line app brief with AI.
3. First build (45 min) - Prompt an app into existence from a starter template and watch it appear live on screen.
4. Iterate & personalise (40 min) - Change colours, copy and features by talking to the AI; learn to give feedback that lands.
5. Ship & show (30 min) - Publish to a shareable link and demo to the group. Everyone leaves with a URL.
sessions.materials: Laptops (own), starter template, speaker and microphone, extension cables

sessions.title: Session 2 - Intermediate AI App Development
sessions.activities:
1. From toy to tool (20 min) - Recap the basics, then read what the AI actually generated so it stops feeling like magic.
2. Design the data (30 min) - Plan what the app needs to remember, then have AI scaffold a database around it.
3. Wire it up (50 min) - Connect storage and pull in a live external API (weather, transit, or a public dataset).
4. Debug like a pro (40 min) - Things break, good. Learn to read errors and pair with AI to fix them quickly.
5. Deploy & demo (40 min) - Ship to the real internet, then present the build and one hard problem solved.
sessions.materials: Laptops (own), speaker and microphone, extension cables

sessions.title: Session 3 - AI in App Design
sessions.activities:
1. Design thinking, fast (25 min) - Pick a cause, define an audience, and frame the design problem. Good design starts before the visuals.
2. Moodboard with AI (30 min) - Generate directions, palettes and references, then curate. Taste is the skill being trained.
3. Brand & visuals (45 min) - Create a logo, key imagery and a poster, learning to art-direct the prompts.
4. Idea to interface (40 min) - Turn the brand into a real landing-page mockup and preview it as a live page.
5. Gallery critique (20 min) - Walk the wall, give and take feedback, the part that builds a designer's eye.
sessions.materials: Laptops (own), speaker and microphone, extension cables

sessions.title: Session 4 - AI in Content Creation
sessions.activities:
1. Message before medium (25 min) - Decide who you're talking to and what you want them to feel. Strategy first, tools second.
2. Script & copy (35 min) - Draft a hook, script and captions with AI, then rewrite in your own voice so it isn't generic.
3. Make the assets (45 min) - Generate visuals, a voiceover and short video clips from the script.
4. Edit & assemble (35 min) - Cut it into a polished 30-60 second piece with captions and music.
5. Showcase reel (20 min) - Play the finished pieces back to back. Everyone leaves with content they can post today.

title: Superstar: ME - A 3-Day Self-Worth Discovery Programme
summary: A 6-session indoor programme over 3 days at Brahm Centre Aljunied that uses games, hands-on activities and guided reflection to help youths discover and celebrate six dimensions of self: Physical, Intellectual, Emotional, Social, Personal and Temporal. Participants build self-worth, emotional regulation, independent thinking, social connection and resilience, and leave with concrete tools such as a Pause Button, calm jar, conversation cards and a worth statement.
objectives: Discover and celebrate six dimensions of self: Physical, Intellectual, Emotional, Social, Personal and Temporal
Sleep Well For Better Focus: understand sleep hygiene and commit to a pre-bed routine (Session 1, Physical)
Think Independently Of Trends: question popular beliefs and weigh opposing views (Session 2, Intellectual)
Regulate Emotions Before Acting: notice, breathe and choose a response (Session 3, Emotional)
Start And Conduct Conversations: open, sustain and close conversations with confidence (Session 4, Social)
Define Self-Worth Beyond Performance: separate who they are from what they achieve (Session 5, Personal)
Embrace Discomfort Without Escape: build resilience by reflecting on past, present and future discomforts (Session 6, Temporal)
facilitators: Main facilitators (depends on session): Jeremy, Lyndon, Mei Jing, Venessa, Xenon, Erwin, Raymond
duration: 3 days, 2 sessions per day (120-150 min per session)
materials: Superstar:ME Journal Booklet (1 per pax, A5, 20 pages, B&W printing, stapled)
Art supplies (markers, coloured pencils, glue, scissors)
Tables and chairs arranged for group work
equipment:
Portable speaker (for music)
Whiteboard/flip-chart stand
Markers
Projector (optional)
Tables and chairs arranged for group work
youthNeed: Today's youths face unprecedented levels of stress, anxiety, and pressure. Record numbers report feeling overwhelmed by academic demands, social media comparison, peer pressure, and uncertainty about their future. Many struggle with low self-worth, tying their value to grades, likes, and external validation. At the same time, they lack safe spaces to explore their identity, process difficult emotions, and build genuine self-confidence. Superstar:ME responds by providing a structured, supportive indoor programme that uses interactive activities and reflection to help youths discover their intrinsic worth and build practical life skills.
whyItMatters: Youths today are not broken—they are navigating an increasingly complex world with fewer built-in supports. Superstar:ME offers a low-cost, high-impact intervention that addresses multiple challenges at once. It builds emotional regulation, self-worth, social confidence, and resilience—all without medication, diagnosis, or digital interface. In a world that constantly asks young people to perform, this programme invites them to simply be—and discover that they are enough, exactly as they are.
competencyHow:
The programme targets all six competencies across its 6 sessions. Primary emphasis is on Define Self-Worth Beyond Performance (through clay sculpting, worth statement, and reflection) and Regulate Emotions Before Acting (through Pause Button creation, calm jars, and role-play), with supporting development of independent thinking, social connection, discomfort tolerance, and sleep awareness.

Participants engage in a carefully sequenced 6-session journey, each targeting one specific competency:

Session 1 (Physical): Sleep hygiene education and Sleep Sanctuary Diorama creation

Session 2 (Intellectual): Independent thinking through "Trend or Truth?" debate and Thought Compass activity

Session 3 (Emotional): Emotional regulation via DIY Pause Button, Calm Jar, and Role-Play Replay

Session 4 (Social): Conversation skills through Toolkit Card Deck creation and role-play practice

Session 5 (Personal): Self-worth exploration through clay sculpture and Worth Statement

Session 6 (Temporal): Discomfort embrace through obstacle course and Courage Capsule creation.

Each session uses hands-on, tactile activities that make abstract concepts concrete and memorable.
icePurposes: Introduce the idea of self-discovery and personal sharing in a low-stakes way
iceSteps:
Participants share three statements about themselves:

1. Each participant writes down or thinks of three statements: - Two statements that are TRUE about themselves (facts, experiences, hobbies) - One statement that is a DREAM or aspiration (something they hope for, wish for, or imagine for their future)

2. Going around the circle, each participant shares all three statements without revealing which is which.

3. The rest of the group guesses which two statements are true and which one is the dream.

4. After guessing, the participant reveals the answers and briefly explains one of their truths or their dream.

Facilitator Note: Emphasise that there are no wrong answers. The dream can be big or small, serious or silly. The goal is to practise sharing and listening in a supportive environment.
iceWhy: Youths often feel pressure to present a "perfect" version of themselves. This activity normalises sharing both realities and aspirations in a fun, game-like format. It encourages vulnerability without requiring deep emotional disclosure, builds group connection through curiosity and laughter, and gently introduces the theme of self-discovery that runs throughout the programme.
mainActivities:
Programme Overview
Superstar:ME is a 6-session self-worth discovery programme delivered across 3 days (2 sessions per day) at Brahm Centre Aljunied. Each session targets one of the six aspects of self (Physical, Intellectual, Emotional, Social, Personal, Temporal) and one core competency. Participants will be guided through a series of games, hands-on activities, and reflective exercises designed to promote positive self-outlook and self-discovery.
Programme Structure
Participants will be first encouraged to store their phones away, either keeping them in their bags or in a designated "keep safe" box for the duration of each session. This allows for full presence and engagement.
Participants will then be introduced to their Superstar:ME Journal Pack, a self-discovery kit consisting of:
A Superstar:ME Journal Booklet (A5, 20 pages)
Coloured markers and pens
Stickers
Activity-specific materials provided per session
After explaining the Journal and its purpose, Facilitators will commence the session, which follows a consistent 4-segment structure:
The Warm-Up (Game): A fun, engaging game to introduce the session's theme
The Main Event (Activity): A hands-on, creative activity to explore that specific aspect of self
The Cool Down (Debrief): A guided reflection and group discussion
The Spotlight (Takeaway): A short, practical action and mantra to carry forward
Each session includes a reflection prompt in the Superstar:ME Journal that participants complete during or after the activity.
Session Activities (6 Sessions Across 3 Days)
Day 1 – Session 1: Physical Self – Sleep Well For Better Focus
The Warm-Up is a movement-based game called Sleepy Statues, where participants dance to music and freeze in sleep-related poses when the music stops. This activity introduces the theme of rest and physical wellbeing in a lighthearted way.
The Main Event is My Sleep Sanctuary – 3D Diorama, where participants build a small diorama of their ideal sleep environment using cardboard boxes, coloured paper, and markers. They include elements like a bed, calming colours, and personal touches. On the back, they write a personal Sleep Pledge listing three things they will do 30 minutes before bed.
The Cool Down is the Sleep Detective Log, where participants receive a weekly sleep log template. The group discusses barriers to good sleep and brainstorms practical solutions together.
The Spotlight is a Takeaway action to set a bedtime alarm 30 minutes before sleep, accompanied by the mantra: "Rest is not weakness. Rest is my superpower for focus."

Day 1 – Session 2: Intellectual Self – Think Independently Of Trends
The Warm-Up is Trend or Truth?, where participants identify whether statements are social media trends or lesser-known facts. This activity encourages critical thinking and questioning of popular beliefs.
The Main Event is The Independent Thinker's Debate, where small groups receive a provocative question. Each member writes their initial opinion, then groups rotate to add counterarguments. They return to review new perspectives and present their final stance, demonstrating how considering opposing views strengthens independent thinking.
The Cool Down is My Thought Compass, where participants complete a compass rose with North (core belief), South (questioned trend), East (new perspective), and West (topic to research).
The Spotlight is a Takeaway action to ask "What is the evidence? What do I think?" when hearing a popular opinion, accompanied by the mantra: "I have my own mind. I think for myself."

Day 2 – Session 3: Emotional Self – Regulate Emotions Before Acting
The Warm-Up is The Emotion Volcano, where participants physically move to a number on the floor representing their emotional reaction intensity to everyday scenarios. They practise taking a deep breath and moving down the scale before speaking.
The Main Event is the DIY Pause Button and Calm Jar. Participants decorate a wooden or cardboard circle as their Pause Button and write a Pause Script on the back: Notice the emotion, Breathe three slow breaths, and Choose a response aligned with their values. They also create a calm jar as a visual metaphor for emotions settling.
The Cool Down is The Replay Reel, where participants pair up and share a recent moment they wish they had handled differently. Their partner asks what they could have done with a pause, and they role-play the new version.
The Spotlight is a Takeaway action to keep the Pause Button visible and physically touch it before reacting, accompanied by the mantra: "I pause. I breathe. I choose."

Day 2 – Session 4: Social Self – Start And Conduct Conversations
The Warm-Up is Conversation Jenga, where participants pull blocks with conversation starters from a Jenga tower and ask the question to the group, practising spontaneous conversation skills.
The Main Event is The Conversation Toolkit – Card Deck, where participants create a card deck with three categories: Openers (ways to start a conversation), Follow-ups (ways to keep it going), and Closers (graceful ways to end). They then pair up and practise a short conversation using only their toolkit cards.
The Cool Down is The Social Map Reflection, where participants draw a social map of their upcoming week, identify one specific situation, and write down which Opener card they will use. They share with a partner and receive encouragement.
The Spotlight is a Takeaway action to start at least one new conversation using a card from the toolkit, accompanied by the mantra: "I have the tools to connect. My voice matters."

Day 3 – Session 5: Personal Self – Define Self-Worth Beyond Performance
The Warm-Up is The Achievement vs. Identity Sort, where participants draw slips of paper with statements and physically place them into two labelled bins: Achievements and Identity. This highlights the difference between what they do and who they are.
The Main Event is The Unshakeable Core – Clay Sculpture, where participants sculpt a core object representing their intrinsic self—something that would remain true even if all achievements and recognition were stripped away. They paint it with a single colour to symbolise its unchanging nature.
The Cool Down is The Worth Statement, where participants write a single sentence declaring their worth independent of performance on a decorative card, placed with their sculpture as a permanent reminder.
The Spotlight is a Takeaway action to place the sculpture and Worth Statement somewhere visible and repeat the statement when measuring worth by outcome, accompanied by the mantra: "My worth is inherent. I am not my performance."

Day 3 – Session 6: Temporal Self – Embrace Discomfort Without Escape
The Warm-Up is The Discomfort Timeline – Human Graph, where participants stand on a rope timeline representing where they feel they currently are in their ability to handle discomfort. They share one thing they have learned from a past uncomfortable experience.
The Main Event is The Discomfort Map – Indoor Obstacle Course, where participants complete a low-key indoor obstacle course with various stations representing different types of discomfort. After completing the course, they create a visual map with symbols for past discomforts survived and future discomforts anticipated, writing beside future symbols: "I survived before. I can face this too."
The Cool Down is The Courage Capsule, where participants write three things on separate slips: one past discomfort that made them stronger, one current discomfort they are facing, and one future discomfort they want to face with courage. They seal and decorate a small container as a reminder of their resilience.
The Spotlight is a Takeaway action to keep the Courage Capsule accessible and hold it when feeling the urge to escape discomfort, accompanied by the mantra: "Discomfort is my teacher. I grow through what I go through."

Adapt to changes, not giving up and relooking when issues arise

title: Mind Craft - Stress Management Programme
summary: An interactive exam-stress workshop for teens that normalises exam anxiety, explains why the brain goes blank under pressure, and teaches silent coping skills for the exam hall plus evidence-based study habits. Participants leave with a personalised, portable toolkit: an Exam Day Blueprint card and a lanyard cue card with their go-to breath, anchor and mantra.
objectives: Normalise exam anxiety and get honest data on participants' biggest fears
Teach the biology of memory retrieval under pressure, and differentiate between pre-exam stress and during-exam stress
Teach coping skills specifically designed for use during an exam, when you cannot leave your seat or make noise
Ditch the all-nighters and teach evidence-based revision techniques that actually reduce stress
Turn knowledge into a personalised, portable toolkit
materials: Spinner/wheel or cards for Revision Roulette
Blank laminated cards + keyrings/string for lanyards
Metronome or phone timer (for breathwork station)
equipment: Whiteboard and markers; speaker; metronome or phone timer
iceSteps:
Place 4 large buckets/bowls at the front labelled "Going Blank / Memory Freeze", "Running Out of Time", "Letting My Parents/Teachers Down" and "Other".
Give each teen 3 ping-pong balls or crumpled paper balls.
Teens throw their balls into the bucket that represents their biggest exam fear.
Facilitator points out that every bucket has balls in it: "You are NOT weird, broken, or alone. The fear of going blank is actually your brain's threat-detector misfiring. Today, we are going to hack that system."
iceWhy: Normalises exam anxiety and gets honest data on their biggest fears.
mainActivities:
Segment 1, Understanding Exam Stress (50 min): Whiteboard vs. Sticky Notes brain demo; Stress Timeline floor map; A+ vs. Pass myth-busting.
Active brain break: The Revision Shake (5 min).
Segment 2, Coping Mechanisms (50 min): Silent SOS stations (Box Breath, Page Pause grounding, Brain-Dump, Micro-Movement release); Worst-Case Scenario roleplay in pairs.
Passive brain break: The 2-Minute Exam Reset guided visualisation (5 min).
Segment 3, Mindfulness and Study Habits (50 min): Pomodoro vs. Marathon race; Revision Roulette; Night-Before and Morning-Of Blueprint card.
Closing: The Exam Day Lanyard cue card and the 10-Minute post-exam rule (10 min).
involvementNotes: Teens walk a floor timeline and place symptom cards, shout out myths, rotate through 4 silent stations every 7 minutes, roleplay in pairs as "Panicked Student" and "Calm Coach", race in two teams, and fill in their own Exam Day Blueprint and lanyard cue card.

sessions.title: Welcome & Ice-Breaker: "The Exam Fear Factor"
sessions.activities:
Place 4 large buckets/bowls at the front labelled "Going Blank / Memory Freeze", "Running Out of Time", "Letting My Parents/Teachers Down", "Other".
Give each teen 3 ping-pong balls or crumpled paper balls; they throw them into the bucket that represents their biggest exam fear.
Facilitator script: "Look at that. Every single bucket has balls in it. You are NOT weird, broken, or alone. The fear of going blank is actually your brain's threat-detector misfiring. Today, we are going to hack that system."
sessions.materials: 4 buckets/bowls with labels, ping-pong balls or crumpled paper (3 per teen)

sessions.title: Segment 1: Understanding Exam Stress - "Why does my brain go blank?"
sessions.activities:
1. The "Whiteboard vs. Sticky Notes" Brain Demo (15 min) - A volunteer gets 5 seconds to remember and write a 10-digit number you shout out (e.g. 7482910563). Debrief: Working Memory (the whiteboard) holds only 3-5 things; stress pumps adrenaline which shrinks the whiteboard. The "Sticky Note" fix: Long-Term Memory (the filing cabinet) is infinite; the trick is retrieval practice, actively pulling information out rather than re-reading.
2. The "Stress Timeline" Floor Map (20 min) - Masking-tape timeline on the floor: 1 Month Before, 1 Week Before, Night Before, Morning of Exam, In the Exam Hall, During the Last 10 Minutes. Teens walk the timeline and place symptom cards (e.g. "Can't sleep", "Heart racing", "Stomach cramps", "Mind goes blank", "Sweaty palms", "Overwhelming urge to check phone") where they feel them most. Debrief: chronic stress (weeks before) depletes energy, acute stress (in the hall) triggers fight/flight; they are treated differently.
3. The "A+ vs. Pass" Myth-Busting (15 min) - Two columns on the board: "What I think I need to do" vs. "What actually works". Teens shout out myths (e.g. "I need to study for 6 hours straight"); debunk with science: after 45 minutes of focus the brain stops retaining info; retrieval practice is 50% more effective than re-reading; nervousness is just energy, reframe it as excitement.
sessions.materials: Whiteboard and marker, masking tape, symptom cards

sessions.title: Active Brain Break: "The Revision Shake"
sessions.activities: Play a fast-paced song. Shout out a subject topic (e.g. "Pythagoras!", "Photosynthesis!"); teens do 5 star-jumps while shouting back ONE fact about it. Physically anchors knowledge to movement.

sessions.title: Segment 2: Coping Mechanisms - "The Exam-Hall Rescue Kit"
sessions.activities:
1. The "Silent SOS" Stations (30 min) - 4 stations, teens rotate every 7 minutes; each technique can be done silently at a desk during an exam.
Station A: The "Box Breath" Reset - 4-4-4-4 breathing (inhale 4, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4) for 2 minutes with a metronome/timer while holding a pencil; do it as soon as the invigilator says "You may begin".
Station B: The "Page Pause" Grounding - palms flat on the desk, feel the surface, press gently, say in your head "This desk is solid. I am solid.", then trace the margin line of the exam paper with a finger.
Station C: The "Brain-Dump" Technique - on spare paper, spend 60 seconds writing everything remembered about a topic before reading the question; practise with a random topic (e.g. "World War 2 causes").
Station D: The "Micro-Movement" Release - ankle rotations under the desk, shoulder shrugs, jaw release.
2. The "Worst-Case Scenario" Roleplay (20 min) - Scenario cards for exam-hall disasters (e.g. "You read Question 5 and you have NO idea what it means", "15 minutes left and 3 essays to write", "The person next to you is sniffing and tapping their pen loudly"). In pairs, a "Panicked Student" and a "Calm Coach" who walks them through a station technique. Key script: "Stop. Breathe. Anchor. Then attack the question you DO know first."
sessions.materials: Metronome or phone timer, pencils, spare paper, laminated scenario/roleplay cards

sessions.title: Passive Brain Break: "The 2-Minute Exam Reset"
sessions.activities: Teens sit upright with eyes closed. Guided visualisation: "Imagine you are sitting in the exam hall. You flip the paper over. Your heart thumps. Now, pause. You place your palms on the desk. You take 3 box breaths. You look at the clock and say to yourself, 'I have time.' You read the first question and underline the keywords. You are calm. You are capable. Open your eyes."

sessions.title: Segment 3: Mindfulness & Study Habits - "Studying Smarter, Not Harder"
sessions.activities:
1. The "Pomodoro vs. Marathon" Race (15 min) - Two teams. Team Marathon writes 1 to 100 without stopping; Team Pomodoro writes 1-20, stands and stretches 30 seconds, then 21-40, and so on. Time them. Debrief: Pomodoro technique, 25 minutes focused revision (phones face down) then a 5-minute active break (walk, stretch, hydrate, no scrolling).
2. The "Revision Roulette" Game (20 min) - Spinner/cards with retrieval techniques: "Blurt it out" (60 seconds on a topic), "Draw it" (diagram/mind-map with no words), "Teach it" (explain like they are 5), "Quiz it" (write 3 exam questions). Spin for a random subject (e.g. Photosynthesis, Quadratic Equations, Macbeth) and revise it on the spot. Script: "Re-reading your notes is like watching a cooking show. Retrieval practice is actually cooking the meal."
3. The "Night-Before & Morning-Of" Blueprint (15 min) - Double-sided Exam Day Blueprint card. Side A, The Night Before: stop-studying time (8 PM max), one relaxing activity, pack your bag now (pens, calculator, water, snack). Side B, The Morning Of: eat protein, 5 minutes of box breathing before leaving, arrive early but avoid panicked friends who are cramming. Keep it in the phone case or pencil case.
sessions.materials: Timer, paper and pens, Revision Roulette spinner/wheel or cards, Exam Day Blueprint cards

sessions.title: Closing & Commitment Ceremony: "The Exam Day Lanyard"
sessions.activities:
The "Lanyard Cue Card": each teen writes ONLY 3 things on a blank laminated card on a string/keyring: My go-to breath (e.g. Box Breath), My anchor (e.g. palms on the desk), My mantra (e.g. "I know more than I think I do."). Wear it as a lanyard or keep it in the pencil case for every exam.
The "Post-Exam" Rule: the 10-Minute Rule, vent to a friend for exactly 10 minutes after an exam, then talk about something else; set a phone timer for it.
Final facilitator script: "Exams don't define your intelligence; they test your ability to retrieve information under artificial pressure. Your body is not your enemy... You have the tools. When you sit down in that hall, you are not alone, you are carrying this entire room with you."

mfFraming: Silent techniques for the exam hall: Box Breath 4-4-4-4 breathing, Page Pause grounding (palms flat on the desk, "This desk is solid. I am solid."), Micro-Movement release, and the 2-Minute Exam Reset guided visualisation with eyes closed.
intendedOutcomes: Participants leave with a personalised, portable toolkit: an Exam Day Blueprint card and a lanyard cue card with their go-to breath, anchor and mantra.
notes:
Key mantra: "Stop. Breathe. Anchor. Then attack the question you DO know first."

Facilitator note on stress types: you cannot use a "calm-down" technique if you haven't been sleeping well for 3 weeks; chronic and acute stress are treated differently.

Missing details: the document is a run-sheet only (no planning form); it has no date, venue, facilitators, group size, budget, core competencies, risk management or evaluation plan. Age band inferred from "teens" and the earlier 13-15 setting.

summary: A customisable baking experience where participants work together in small groups to create Granola Power Bars (granola cups), choosing their own add-ins and toppings. It gives youths a safe space to make self-directed decisions, experiment and make mistakes, and builds agency, communication and basic kitchen life skills. Youths should leave with a greater sense of achievement and better self-confidence.

Engage with peers through a mix of group and individual activities, building communicative and innovative skills
Equip participants with life skills in food preparation and basic kitchen usage

youthNeed:
The main challenge being targeted is the youth's need for agency and autonomy. By encouraging them to make self-directed decisions, these individuals are able to practise being independent without external pressure or influence.

The safe space provided in the centre allows participants to experiment, explore and make mistakes in a controlled and non-threatening space. The participants will be provided opportunities to engage with peers through a mix of group and individual activities, allowing them to engage in a social setting and building their communicative and innovative skills.

The activity also aims to equip participants with life skills in food preparation and basic kitchen usage.
whyItMatters:
Youths in this age group often lack the opportunity to explore and express themselves through different mediums. It is a critical period of their life to build a stable self-identity and image. It is also the period where individuals are the most curious and open to changes. By restricting their options, it will hinder their willingness to try out new experiences in the future.

It is also at the age where the brain is the most flexible; by incorporating a novel environment where they are allowed to explore freely, it helps develop the brain, expanding its capability to learn and adapt.

Basic life skills will empower these youths to have a better grasp of their internal sense of autonomy.

Competency in preparing and creating the dish
Greater confidence in self
Building of self-identity and autonomy

title: Masquerade Mystery – Ex Alumni Christmas Programme
summary: A warm and welcoming Christmas masquerade gathering that bridges the past and the future of the youth community, inviting former interns to reconnect, share stories and reignite old friendships while meeting the newest youth team members. Through casual icebreakers, sharing circles and free-flowing conversation, young adults build social confidence, a sense of belonging and fresh connections.
objectives: Reconnect former interns, share stories and reignite old friendships
Help former interns meet and mingle with the newest youth team members
Build interpersonal communication: initiating conversations, active listening and articulating personal stories
Foster a sense of belonging by bridging past interns with new members, reinforcing that everyone is valued regardless of tenure
Cultivate empathy and awareness through sharing and listening to others' stories

Jeremy, Raymond – main staff on site
Lyndon, Mei Jing, Xenon – care staff on site

youthNeed:
Sense of belonging and community: many young people today face isolation and a lack of meaningful social connections, especially post-pandemic. They seek safe, inclusive spaces where they feel seen, valued, and part of a supportive tribe.
Continuity and purpose: after completing internships or programmes, youth often experience a "drop-off" in engagement, losing touch with peers and mentors. They need ongoing touchpoints to maintain relationships and feel their contributions still matter.
Mentorship and peer learning: young people crave opportunities to learn from those who've walked similar paths, both older peers and newcomers. Exposure to diverse experiences helps them navigate their own journeys with more confidence.
Emotional safety and validation: youth need environments where they can share authentically without judgment, reflect on their growth, and feel that their past efforts are acknowledged and celebrated.
Transition support: as they move between life stages (e.g. internship to work, school to gap year), youth benefit from networks that offer guidance, encouragement, and a soft landing as they figure out their next steps.
whyItMatters: These needs are not "nice-to-haves"; they are essential for healthy youth development. Addressing them builds resilience, fosters emotional well-being, and creates a generation of young people who are connected, confident, and ready to contribute meaningfully to their communities.
competencyHow: Primary focus as written on the form: interpersonal communication. Through structured icebreakers like "Behind the Mask" and Human Bingo, participants practise initiating conversations, active listening, and articulating personal stories, building confidence in social and professional interactions.
iceSteps:
1. Inside your group: each person takes 2 minutes to share their alias name and their connection to the team (current role, past internship, or how they're involved), and the inspiration behind their mask or costume (why they chose it, what it represents, or if it reflects a hidden talent, personality trait, or favourite character).
2. Group introduction: after everyone in the group has shared, the group selects one representative to introduce all 5 members to the rest of the participants (or the wider room), briefly sharing each person's name and team connection and one memorable highlight from each person's mask or costume story.
3. Rotation (optional): if time permits, groups can rotate and mix after 15-20 minutes, allowing participants to meet new people beyond their initial group.
iceWhy:
Encourages mature self-expression: at 17-25, young adults are refining their personal identity. The masquerade theme gives them creative freedom to express their personality and values through costume choices, without feeling childish or forced.
Builds social and networking confidence: this age group is navigating internships, higher education, and early careers. The structured small-group format provides a low-stakes opportunity to practise introducing themselves and articulating their thoughts, skills that transfer directly to professional and social settings.
Balances fun with meaningful connection: the costume element provides an instant, interesting conversation starter, helping participants skip awkward small talk and dive into authentic storytelling.
mainActivities:
Human Bingo:
1. Prepare the cards: a 5x5 Bingo card for each participant with 25 fun, inclusive icebreaker statements (e.g. "Has worn a costume before", "Speaks two or more languages", "Has been to a masquerade"), with a FREE SPACE in the centre.
2. Distribute and explain: hand out one card and a pen to each participant. The goal is to mingle and find someone who matches each statement and have that person sign the square. No one may sign their own card.
3. Set the timer: announce a time limit (e.g. 20-25 minutes) to circulate, introduce themselves and collect signatures from as many different people as possible.
4. Start mingling: participants approach others with a friendly introduction, then ask if they fit a square. If yes, they sign; if no, move on to someone else.
5. Call "BINGO!": on completing a row, column or diagonal, the participant shouts "BINGO!" and comes to the front. The facilitator verifies the signatures by having them briefly introduce the people who signed each square.
6. Continue or wrap up: announce additional winners for a full house if time permits, then gather everyone back to debrief. A few participants share one interesting thing they learned about someone new.
involvementNotes: Every youth present is an active player, moving around the room, initiating conversations, and collecting signatures. They are not passive observers; they are constantly interacting, listening, and sharing stories, which keeps them fully engaged throughout the game.

Group introduction: after everyone has shared, the group selects one representative to introduce all 5 members to the wider room, briefly sharing each person's name and team connection and one memorable highlight from each person's mask or costume story
Rotation (optional): if time permits, groups rotate and mix after 15-20 minutes to meet new people beyond their initial group

intendedOutcomes: The Masquerade Ball aims to build social confidence by encouraging youths to initiate conversations, introduce themselves, and articulate personal stories through structured icebreakers like Human Bingo and "Behind the Mask." It fosters a sense of belonging by bridging past interns with new members through inclusive activities and shared festive experiences, reinforcing that everyone is valued regardless of tenure. It cultivates empathy and awareness by inviting participants to share the inspiration behind their costumes and listen to others' stories, promoting active listening, perspective-taking, and appreciation for diverse backgrounds.
